passage: I'm Seema, and I sat two rows behind Jomon at the class movie about the haunted house. When the music turned creepy, Jomon pulled his knees up and wrapped both arms round himself, chin on his knees. I couldn't tell if he was scared or cold because the air conditioner was on. I leaned forward and whispered, “You okay?” He said, “Just cold. And a bit scared.” I gave him my school sweater to hold. He nodded and held it against his chest for the rest of the film, still watching.

qa.q: Where was Seema sitting compared with Jomon at the movie?
qa.a: Seema was sitting two rows behind Jomon.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he hugged himself, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: A bit scared by the creepy music, and cold too, as he told Seema. Seema could not tell which at first, since both fit.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped?
qa.a: Seema whispered a quiet check-in instead of assuming, and offered her sweater to hold, so Jomon could say how he felt.

qa.q: How might Seema feel watching Jomon hug himself?
qa.a: Seema was probably concerned for Jomon, leaning forward to check and then handing over the school sweater.

grounding: A child hugs himself for comfort during a scary film; a quiet check-in beats assuming.

passage:
Monday: at lunch, Jahnavi sat hugging her rag doll to her chest after a quarrel with her friend. Her classmate Rafiq noticed, sat on the next bench and quietly opened his tiffin. He said nothing.
Wednesday: at the bus stop on a cold morning, Jahnavi stood with her arms wrapped round herself. Rafiq asked, “Cold, or something else?” “Both, a bit,” she said. He offered her half his scarf.
Friday: Jahnavi's arms were swinging by her sides. She was telling Rafiq about the quiz, and she laughed.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi hugging at lunch on Monday?
qa.a: She was hugging her rag doll to her chest.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday, and what else might the hugging show?
qa.a: Probably upset after the quarrel with her friend, so she soothed herself with the doll. It may also hint at worry, since she stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that respected Jahnavi at each stage?
qa.a: On Monday he sat nearby and said nothing, and on Wednesday he asked a gentle question and offered half his scarf, so she could answer in her own way.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel seeing Jahnavi hug her doll after the quarrel?
qa.a: Rafiq was probably concerned but careful not to push, since he sat on the next bench and said nothing.

grounding: Hugging oneself or a soft toy soothes after upset; a quiet check-in helps more than assuming.

passage: Ujjwal, you're squeezing that cushion like I used to squeeze myself. Let your Ayesha Khala tell you. When I was nine, a big storm knocked out the power in our Lucknow house. I sat on the stairs with my arms wrapped tight round my own body, rocking a little. My sister said, “She's cold, get her a shawl.” My father sat down beside me without a word. After a while he asked, very quietly, “Cold, or scared, or both?” I said, “Scared of the thunder.” He didn't laugh. He counted the seconds between flash and bang with me, and as they grew longer, my arms loosened.

qa.q: What knocked out the power in the Lucknow house?
qa.a: A big storm knocked out the power.

qa.q: What was young Ayesha feeling as she hugged herself on the stairs?
qa.a: She was scared of the thunder, as she told her father, though her sister thought she was just cold.

qa.q: What choice did her father make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He sat quietly and asked whether she was cold, scared or both, then counted the thunder with her, which soothed her without assuming.

qa.q: How did Ayesha's sister read the self-hug?
qa.a: Her sister thought Ayesha was cold and suggested a shawl, which shows the same hug could have more than one reason.

grounding: Shows a child hugging herself for comfort during a storm, and a quiet check-in working better than assuming the cause.

passage: The overnight train to Kolkata was packed, and the man in the next berth had been shouting into his phone for an hour. Parveen sat on the upper berth with her old grey rabbit squeezed against her chest, arms wrapped round it and her knees. Minakshi Mashi, on the lower berth, noticed. Was she cold? The fan was blasting. Or was the shouting getting to her? Minakshi climbed halfway up and spoke under the noise. “Want a shawl, or just some quiet?” Parveen hugged the rabbit tighter. “Quiet. He sounds angry.” Minakshi handed up her earplugs and her shawl anyway, and sat where Parveen could see her until the rabbit loosened.

qa.q: Where was the train going?
qa.a: The overnight train was going to Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling as she squeezed the rabbit?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little scared of the angry shouting, though the blasting fan might have made her cold too.

qa.q: Why was Minakshi's question better than guessing?
qa.a: Asking “shawl, or just some quiet?” let Parveen name the real cause, so Minakshi could offer earplugs, a shawl and her presence.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt watching from the lower berth?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably concerned and unsure what the hug meant, which is why she climbed up to check.

grounding: Shows a child hugging a soft toy for comfort, which could mean cold or worry, and a quiet check-in finding the cause.

passage: At Swati's birthday sleepover in her Bengaluru flat, the girls voted for a scary film. Halfway through, when a door in the film creaked open, Aadhya pulled her knees up and wrapped both arms tight round them, chin tucked in. Swati noticed from the other end of the sofa. Aadhya wasn't screaming or laughing like the others, just holding herself very still. Swati slid over. “Popcorn run?” she whispered. In the kitchen she asked, “Too scary, or just cold? The AC's freezing.” Aadhya let out a breath. “Bit of both.” Swati handed her a hoodie. “Let's put on the funny one next. I'll say it's a birthday rule.”

qa.q: Whose birthday sleepover was it?
qa.a: It was Swati's birthday sleepover.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling as she wrapped her arms round her knees?
qa.a: She was frightened by the film and also cold from the freezing AC, and holding herself helped her feel safer.

qa.q: What did Swati do to check in without embarrassing Aadhya?
qa.a: She invited Aadhya on a popcorn run and asked in the kitchen, away from the others, then offered a hoodie and a funnier film.

qa.q: What might the other girls have thought if Swati had asked in front of everyone?
qa.a: They might have teased Aadhya for being scared, which would have made her feel embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child hugging herself during a scary film, which could also mean cold, and a quiet check-in instead of assuming.

passage:
"Santosh, why are you all wrapped up like a samosa?"
"I'm not."
"You've got both arms round yourself and Bhalu squashed under your chin."
"…The ghost part's coming."
Akash bhaiya paused the film. "Cold, or scared?"
"Bit of both. The fan's on full."
"Want me to switch the film off?"
"No! I want to see how it ends."
"Okay. Fan down, shawl on, and I'll sit right here. If it gets too much, we stop. No teasing."
"Promise no teasing?"
"Promise."
Santosh loosened one arm, just enough to hold the edge of the shawl.

qa.q: What was Santosh holding under his chin?
qa.a: Bhalu, squashed under his chin.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling as he hugged himself and Bhalu?
qa.a: A bit scared of the coming ghost part and a bit cold from the fan, as he admits; the hug was his way of soothing himself.

qa.q: What made Akash bhaiya's check-in work?
qa.a: He asked a quiet question, "Cold, or scared?", instead of assuming or teasing, then fixed the cold and stayed close 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Akash bhaiya had laughed at the "samosa" and kept the film going?
qa.a: Santosh might hide the fear, feel ashamed and scared alone, and be less likely to say what he needs next time.

grounding: It shows a child hugging himself and a soft toy during a scary film, and an older brother checking in quietly instead of assuming.
